what_it_does: Solid-state drives (SSDs) store data in flash memory cells, and over time they must reclaim space by erasing and rewriting blocks — a process called garbage collection. A key problem is "write amplification": to erase one block, the drive must first copy all the still-valid data elsewhere, causing far more actual writes than the host requested, which wastes time and wears out the drive faster. One known remedy is "streaming" — grouping data with similar lifetimes together so they can be erased cleanly — but existing stream-management solutions require the host computer to label data, which application developers rarely do. StreamCSD instead runs entirely inside the drive. It notices that data which compresses to similar ratios tends to have similar lifetimes (an observation about content similarity), and uses that signal — already available from compressors built into computational storage drives (storage chips that can also run code) — to cluster incoming data into streams automatically, without any host involvement. The approach is plausible and novel in framing, but the full paper is needed to confirm accuracy and real-world write-amplification gains.
